quote: Add one bit to the key and the work doubles; double the number of bits and it squares.
problem: This sentence comes straight after 'Factoring is kinder... each extra bit costs less than a doubling', so it reads as a rule for RSA keys and contradicts the sentence before it. It is also wrong for curve keys: Section 05 (fig-14-9 strip, fig-14-10 strip) says a 256-bit curve key gives about 128 bits of work, because a square-root search means twice the bits only square the work. The paragraph's closing 'At 256 bits of key' then suggests 2^256 work for a 256-bit key, which goes against the 256-to-128 table in Fig 14.10. The rule holds only for a brute-force search through keys.
fix: Move the sentence to just after 'roughly O(2^n).' and scope it: 'For a search through every possible key, add one bit and the work doubles; double the number of bits and it squares.' Then 'Factoring is kinder...' follows as written. Change 'At 256 bits of key' to 'At 2^256 steps'.
reason: ch14-primer-p6 puts 'Add one bit to the key and the work doubles' straight after the sentence saying factoring is kinder than a doubling per bit, so it reads as a rule for RSA keys. 'At 256 bits of key' then suggests 2^256 work, against Fig 14.10 (256-bit curve = 128 bits of work). The rule is true only for a search through every key.
judge_fix: Reorder and scope: '...exponential: roughly O(2^n). For a search through every possible key, add one bit and the work doubles; double the number of bits and it squares. Factoring is kinder, called sub-exponential: each extra bit costs less than a doubling, which is why an RSA key needs thousands of bits where an elliptic-curve key needs 256, yet its cost still outgrows any power of n. At 2^256 steps (a full search of a 256-bit key), "hard" is several orders of magnitude beyond the entire computational capacity of Earth running until the heat death of the universe.'

quote: in ECDSA and Ed25519 (the schemes TLS 1.3 actually uses)
problem: This says TLS 1.3 uses only the curve signatures. The same section's figure strip lists 'Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA-PSS for the server's signature', and Section 04 says the same (ch14-publickey-p6: 'the long-term RSA or ECDSA key only for signing'; fig-14-8 strip: 'where it appears it only signs'). Ch11's example chain (R11, ISRG Root X1) is RSA.
fix: Replace the parenthesis with '(which TLS 1.3 uses alongside RSA-PSS)'.
reason: ch14-tls-pqc-p3 says ECDSA and Ed25519 are 'the schemes TLS 1.3 actually uses'. The Fig 14.11 strip lists 'Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA-PSS', ch14-publickey-p6 says 'RSA or ECDSA key only for signing', and Ch11's chain is RSA. TLS 1.3 does require RSA-PSS support.
judge_fix: Replace the parenthesis: 'in ECDSA and Ed25519 (which TLS 1.3 uses alongside RSA-PSS) it is a different curve computation with the same shape.'

quote: The defence is clean and absolute: never build queries by string concatenation.
problem: Chapter 13 calls parameterised queries a clean and absolute defence, under the heading 'The fix · parameterised queries · and only that'. Chapter 15 then opens its account of the same defence with 'Parameterised queries are necessary but not sufficient'. Fig 15.5's own strip resolves it ('Layer 2 is the real fix; the others exist for the day it is missing'), but the prose sentence contradicts Ch13 head-on.
fix: ch15-web-p2: replace 'Parameterised queries are necessary but not sufficient, so the discipline is' with 'Parameterised queries are the cure wherever they are used; the danger is the one endpoint that skips them, so the discipline is'.
reason: ch13-injection-p4 calls parameterised queries 'clean and absolute' and the section is headed 'and only that'. ch15-web-p2 then opens the same defence with 'necessary but not sufficient'. The Fig 15.5 strip ('Layer 2 is the real fix') resolves it, but the two prose sentences disagree. Change Ch15, since Ch13's claim is the correct one.
judge_fix: ch15-web-p2: 'Parameterised queries are the cure wherever they are used; the danger is the one endpoint that skips them, so the discipline is *defence in depth*: assume every other layer might be bypassed and design each layer as if it were the last one.'

quote: The attacks here are about confused deputies.
problem: The sentence before lists three attacks, the third being 'a backend rebuilding objects from data a visitor sent' (deserialisation), and then calls them all confused deputies. ch15-web-p6 and Fig 15.9 file deserialisation under data-as-code, not confused deputy. The same paragraph later says the attacks reduce to two shapes.
fix: Replace 'The attacks here are about _confused deputies_. A confused deputy is code that has authority...' with 'The first two are _confused deputies_: code that has authority to do something, tricked into using that authority on the attacker's behalf. The third is data the backend ends up running as code.'
reason: ch15-web-p1 lists three scenarios (CSRF-like, SSRF, deserialisation) and says 'The attacks here are about confused deputies'. ch15-web-p6 and Fig 15.9 file deserialisation under data-as-code. The paragraph's last sentence also says two shapes.
judge_fix: Replace 'The attacks here are about _confused deputies_. A confused deputy is code that has authority to do something, tricked into using that authority on the attacker's behalf.' with 'The first two are _confused deputies_: code that has authority to do something, tricked into using that authority on the attacker's behalf. The third is data the backend ends up running as code.' Then reorder the closing clause to match: '...reduce to two of the six shapes this chapter closes on: a deputy confused, or data parsed as code.'

quote: Six structural attack patterns now name every specific exploit in this book.
problem: ch15-culture-p1 adds a habit that is not one of the six: 'ROP (Chapter 3) and Stuxnet (Section 05) show a further habit: chaining pieces the attacker did not write'. Neither ROP nor Stuxnet appears in the six-pattern map (Fig 15.9). Nor does denial of service (SYN floods, Chapter 10, which the Ch15 hero lists among the book's attacks). The 'every' in p7 (and 'Every attack' in p1) is therefore false by the chapter's own account. p1 also lists 'SSRF (this chapter), and the Capital One breach' as if they were two examples, but Capital One is the SSRF example (ch15-web-p4).
fix: p7: 'Six structural attack patterns now name most of the exploits in this book.' p1: 'Almost every attack in this book is...' and 'CSRF (Chapter 12) and SSRF (this chapter, the Capital One breach) are confused-deputy attacks'. Fig 15.9 is kept-original and stays.
reason: ch15-culture-p1 says 'Every attack in this book' fits a handful of patterns, then adds ROP and Stuxnet as 'a further habit' that is not one of the six. ch15-culture-p7 says the six 'name every specific exploit'. Denial of service (SYN floods) is not in the map either. The 'every' is false by the chapter's own account. Capital One is the SSRF example, so listing it separately is sloppy.
judge_fix: p7: 'Six structural attack patterns now name most of the exploits in this book.' p1: 'Almost every attack in this book is, at the structural level, an instance of a small handful of patterns.' and 'CSRF (Chapter 12) and SSRF (this chapter, as in the Capital One breach) are confused-deputy attacks: code with privilege, tricked into using its privilege at the attacker's behest.' Fig 15.9's title and caption (p2: 'underneath every specific attack') are kept-original; flag them to the owner as the same overclaim.

quote: O(|R| × |S|), yet the right choice when one side is tiny

judge_fix: ch13-sql-p4: after 'costs N×M row-comparisons' add '(engineers write such a cost O(N×M): the work grows with the product of the two row counts)'. ch13-indexes-p1: start the parenthesis 'In the same notation, the cost of a full scan is O(N): the work grows in step with the number of rows, N. The structures below cut it to O(log N), one more step each time the table multiplies in size, or O(1), about the same whatever the size.'

quote: It must satisfy three security properties.
problem: Chapter 11 told the reader 'Three properties matter: determinism, preimage resistance, avalanche effect' and called a hash a fingerprint 'uniquely identifying' the data. Chapter 14 gives a different three (preimage, second preimage, collision) and shows that collisions exist at 2^128 work, so 'uniquely' was not true. The two lists of 'three properties' do not line up.
fix: ch14-hashing-p1: 'It must satisfy three security properties, of which Chapter 11 met only the first.' ch11-crypto-p4: replace 'uniquely identifying it' with 'identifying it for every practical purpose'.
reason: ch11-crypto-p4 calls a hash a fingerprint 'uniquely identifying' the data. Ch14 shows collisions exist (found at about 2^128 work, and for SHA-1 in practice). Only the 'uniquely' is wrong. The two 'three properties' lists differ because Ch14's are the security properties and Ch11's mix in determinism and avalanche, so ch14-hashing-p1 needs no change.
judge_fix: ch11-crypto-p4: replace 'uniquely identifying it without revealing it' with 'identifying it for every practical purpose without revealing it'.

quote: the log is immutable in practice
problem: Chapter 11 said Git still uses SHA-1. ch14-hashing-p1 calls SHA-1 'now-broken', and the fig-14-3 strip says collisions were produced in 2017. The reader is then told Git's log is immutable in practice with no word on why a broken hash is still safe here.
fix: 'the log is immutable in practice, even on SHA-1, since forging a commit needs a second preimage, not a collision'
reason: A reader is told SHA-1 is 'now-broken' (collisions in 2017), that Git still uses it (Ch11), then that Git's log is 'immutable in practice'. The loose end is real. The finding's proposed reason (a second preimage, not a collision) is wrong: a collision lets an attacker prepare two objects in advance. The real answer is that Git detects the known collision attacks (SHA-1DC checks; the installed git 2.54 contains 'SHA-1 appears to be part of a collision attack') and supports SHA-256 repositories (git init --object-format=sha256 works).
judge_fix: '...breaks every descendant: the log is immutable in practice (Git still uses SHA-1, with checks that catch the known collision attacks, and can now use SHA-256 instead).'
